claims.label: Overproduction makes a struggle for existence inevitable
claims.statement: Because all organisms tend to increase at a high (geometrical) rate, more individuals are produced than can survive, so every species must undergo a struggle for existence with members of its own species, with other species, or with physical conditions.

operationalizations.text: Calculate intrinsic rates of natural increase (r_max > 0 or lifetime fecundity R_0 >> 1 under uncrowded conditions) alongside realized long-term population growth rates (r ≈ 0) and density-dependent/abiotic mortality fractions across wild plant and animal populations.

Compare potential population growth from fecundity and survival schedules with observed long-run abundance, and quantify density-, enemy- or environment-dependent mortality. Potential production exceeding realized recruitment with limiting mortality supports the mechanism.

Compare potential population growth at low density, from fecundity and survival schedules, with realized long-term abundance. Potential growth well above replacement, with realized numbers checked by conspecifics, other species, or physical factors, would support the argument; life histories whose maximum growth is at or below replacement would refute universal geometrical overproduction.

obstacles: Directly partitioning the exact causes of mortality (intraspecific vs interspecific vs abiotic) is unavailable for many populations in broad demographic databases.
Microbes and many invertebrates are underrepresented.
'Struggle' requires mapping to measurable density dependence or mortality.
The struggle is said to be with conspecifics, other species, or physical conditions, a disjunction that covers every possible check.
Demographic matrices are biased toward plants, vertebrates, and temperate studies.
Potential growth estimated from a short study can misrepresent the long-run tendency to increase.

claims.label: Habits can change without corresponding change of structure
claims.statement: Species sometimes have habits that do not match their structure, such as upland geese with webbed feet that rarely enter water or ground-living woodpeckers, showing that habits can change before structure changes.

operationalizations.text: Map ecological/behavioural traits (e.g. terrestrial vs aquatic foraging stratum, ground vs arboreal habits) and corresponding anatomical structures (e.g. foot webbing, zygodactyl toe morphology, beak shape) onto time-calibrated phylogenies to identify lineages where behavioural niche transitions precede anatomical loss or modification (behavioural drive / phylogenetic lag).

Identify species whose observed habitat use or behaviour differs from that predicted by homologous structures and close relatives, then reconstruct whether behavioural shifts precede structural evolution. Repeated behavioural mismatch with retained ancestral anatomy supports the claim.

Score species whose diet or foraging habitat conflicts with locomotor morphology, such as webbed feet with terrestrial foraging or climbing morphology with ground foraging. Repeated mismatches would confirm that habit and structure can come apart; a scoring rule under which essentially no species mismatch would refute the existential claim. A static mismatch does not show that habit changed first.

obstacles: Continuous partial modifications of bone proportions (e.g. longer tarsi in ground-foraging woodpeckers or reduced webbing in Hawaiian geese) often accompany behavioural shifts, even while major qualitative characters (webbed feet, picid skull/zygodactyly) are retained.
Structure-function mismatch requires an explicit expectation model.
Present-day mismatch does not by itself establish the temporal order of habit and structural change.
What counts as a mismatch between habit and structure needs an explicit coding rule.
The order of change, habit before structure, is not identified by a present-day mismatch.
EltonTraits records species-level habits, not individual flexibility.

claims.label: Neuter insects of one nest should show graded structural differences
claims.statement: If worker modifications spread gradually through selection of fertile parents, sterile workers of the same species in the same nest should sometimes show gradations of structure, and such gradations are in fact often found.

operationalizations.text: Measure continuous morphometric traits (head width, mandible length, thorax length, ocellus development) across sterile workers sampled from single colonies across ant species, and test for unimodal continuous or continuous allometric distributions connecting minor and major worker morphologies within nests.

Measure worker morphology within nests and test whether trait distributions contain continuous or graded intermediates between worker forms. Frequent within-nest intermediates support the prediction; consistently discrete distributions across adequately sampled species oppose it.

Within single nests, test whether worker size and shape are continuously graded or fall into discrete modes, and estimate how often graded nests occur across species. Frequent within-nest gradations confirm the empirical clause; exclusively discrete castes with no graded species would refute the 'often' claim.

obstacles: Static morphometric gradations within a single nest are proximal results of nutritional/hormonal developmental reaction norms, so while their existence is easily confirmed, linking them to ongoing evolutionary transition requires cross-species phylogenetic comparison.
Specimen records may not always preserve nest identity.
Developmental plasticity can produce grades without documenting their evolutionary origin.
Many AntWeb specimens lack a same-nest identifier, so within-nest series must be filtered by hand.
Continuous variation can be nutrition rather than the selective gradation the theory invokes.
Bees, wasps, and termites are far less measured than ants.

claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.label: In later geological periods new species have roughly balanced extinctions
claims.statement: The number of species has not increased indefinitely, at least in the later geological periods, so the production of new forms has caused the extinction of about the same number of old forms.

operationalizations.text: Compare per-interval origination and extinction rates and test for diversity-dependent equilibrium (bounded versus unbounded Cenozoic standing diversity) using shareholder quorum subsampling on global fossil occurrences.

Estimate sampling-standardized global diversity, origination, and extinction rates across later geological intervals. Test whether long-run net diversification is near zero and whether origination covaries with losses, while separating balance from causation.

Compare sampling-standardized origination and extinction counts, and the trend in standing diversity, through the Cenozoic and other later Phanerozoic intervals. Matched gains and losses with flat diversity would support a balance; a sustained rise in diversity would count against it.

obstacles: The Pull of the Recent and greater preservation of young unlithified sediments can create an apparent Cenozoic diversity surge if not fully corrected by subsampling.
Global species richness is incompletely sampled.
Rate balance does not show that new forms caused extinctions.
Different standardizations still disagree about whether later diversity is flat or rising.
Later geological periods is an elastic interval, and global species richness is not observed directly.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.label: Higher taxonomic ranks are almost arbitrary
claims.statement: The relative value of groups such as orders, sub-orders, families, sub-families and genera is, at least at present, almost arbitrary, as shown by groups being raised in rank merely because more allied species were discovered.

operationalizations.text: Test whether clades assigned to the same Linnaean rank (e.g. genus, family, order) exhibit huge, overlapping variance in crown age, molecular divergence, and phenotypic disparity across the tree of life, and whether rank elevation historically correlates with species richness rather than standardized divergence.

Measure variation among taxonomic authorities and through time in rank assignments for equivalent clades, and test whether added species richness predicts rank elevation independent of clade age or divergence. High instability supports arbitrariness, though no dataset can define how much instability counts as 'almost arbitrary.'

For genera, families and orders, measure the spread of crown ages, species richness and morphological disparity within each rank, and test whether ranks occupy distinct, non-overlapping bands. The claim is confirmed if within-rank spreads dwarf the differences between adjacent ranks, and refuted if a rank consistently marks a similar age or amount of difference across classes.

obstacles: Part of the claim is conceptual (that taxonomic rank has no intrinsic ontological metric), though its empirical manifestations—lack of consistent divergence thresholds and sensitivity to species discovery—are directly measurable.
Arbitrariness is a normative concept without a unique threshold.
Historical taxonomic versions are not uniformly digitized.
'Almost arbitrary' has no sharp numerical cutoff, so a weak average rise in age from genus to order can be read either way.
Ranks are more nearly commensurate inside one class than they are across animals and plants together.
Some rank changes really do follow the discovery of more allied species, but the historical revision record is less complete than the current ages.

claims.label: The closest-competing neighbours tend to belong to different genera and orders
claims.statement: Where organisms compete most closely, as on a small patch of ground, the advantages of diversification mean that the coexisting inhabitants generally belong to different genera and orders.

operationalizations.text: Calculate species-to-genus ratios (S/G) and standardized effect sizes of Mean Nearest Taxon Distance (MNTD) or Mean Pairwise Distance (MPD) in small-scale co-occurring quadrat plots compared against regional species pool null models; taxonomic/phylogenetic overdispersion at fine spatial scales confirms the claim.

Compare observed genus- and order-level diversity within standardized small plots to null communities preserving richness and regional species pools. Consistent phylogenetic overdispersion and higher coexistence among distant taxa support the claim; clustering or null structure refutes it.

In small plots, compare the mean taxonomic or phylogenetic distance of co-occurring species with draws from the regional species pool. Excess membership in different genera and orders, relative to that null, would confirm the claim; co-occurrence as related as the null, or more related, would refute it.

obstacles: Environmental filtering at intermediate scales often causes closely related species to co-occur (phylogenetic clustering), opposing the competitive overdispersion predicted at the finest neighbourhood scales.
Taxonomic ranks (genus, order) are somewhat arbitrary across clades, though continuous phylogenetic distance provides an objective modern equivalent.
Co-occurrence does not prove that listed organisms compete most closely.
Plot grain and regional-pool choice affect null-model results.
Without a regional null, any diverse plot belongs to multiple genera by arithmetic.
Habitat filtering can increase relatedness and offset a competition effect.

claims.label: Very few species of past periods have living descendants
claims.statement: Like a tree in which only a few early twigs grew into surviving branches, very few of the species that lived in long-past geological periods now have living modified descendants, and many whole orders, families and genera have died out entirely.

operationalizations.text: Query global fossil occurrence databases across geological eras to calculate the proportion of Paleozoic and Mesozoic orders, families, and genera that are entirely extinct today versus those with extant representatives, and fit birth-death branching models to estimate the fraction of ancient species that leave living descendants.

For clades with fossil-calibrated trees, estimate the fraction of past species or lineages with extant descendants and count complete extinction of higher taxa. A small surviving fraction and many wholly extinct clades support the claim.

Join fossil occurrences in deep time bins to living checklists and phylogenies, and compute the fraction of species, genera, families, and orders with any living descendant lineage. A very small species fraction and a large number of wholly extinct higher taxa would confirm the claim; survival of a large share of ancient species-lineages, or rarity of higher-taxon extinction, would refute it.

obstacles: Paraphyletic taxonomic definitions can make an ancestral genus or family appear 'extinct' via pseudoextinction even when modified descendant clades survive, requiring phylogenetic clade-level checks alongside taxonomic counts.
Soft-bodied organisms are underrepresented in the fossil record.
Most fossil species cannot be assigned as direct ancestors.
The denominator of all species that lived is unknown because fossil sampling is incomplete.
Species-level ancestor-descendant links are almost never resolved, so higher taxa stand in for them.
The fossil record samples a biased subset of past species.
Extinct names can hide surviving lineages that were reclassified.

claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.label: A single formation is likely shorter than the time needed to transform a species
claims.statement: Although each geological formation represents a long lapse of years, each is probably short compared with the time required to change one species into another, so a single formation should rarely contain a full graded series between species.

operationalizations.text: Compare the empirical distribution of single geological formation durations (in Myr, from Macrostrat) against the empirical distribution of fossil species durations / waiting times to speciation (in Myr, from the Paleobiology Database and TimeTree).

Compare durations of formations with independently estimated species-transition durations and measure the frequency of within-formation ancestor-descendant morphological series. Predominantly shorter formations and rare complete series support the claim.

Compare the duration of individual formations with observed species durations and with molecular estimates of time to speciation. Formations systematically shorter than speciation times would support the claim and the expectation that one formation rarely holds a full graded series; formation durations as long as species transformations would count against it.

obstacles: Whether a formation is shorter or longer than a species transition depends on the taxonomic group (e.g., mammal species turn over faster than bivalve species) and how broadly a 'formation' is defined stratigraphically.
Formation boundaries and durations vary regionally.
Speciation duration is hard to estimate independently of fossil sampling.
Observed species durations are truncated and extended by sampling, so they are a biased clock for speciation.
A formation can be short and still capture a rapid local transition.
Molecular speciation intervals and fossil durations measure different things.

claims.label: Bat flight arose from an apparatus for gliding
claims.statement: Bats were derived from gliding animals, and the wing membrane extending to the tail and hind legs in some bats is a trace of an apparatus originally built for gliding rather than flight.

operationalizations.text: Perform aerodynamic modelling, morphometric ordination, and phylogenetic ancestral state reconstruction on Eocene stem bats (e.g. *Onychonycteris finneyi*, *Icaronycteris index*) and crown chiropteran wing membrane attachments (including the uropatagium) to test whether basal bats show gliding-adapted intermediate morphology and whether the hind-leg/tail membrane is ancestrally retained from a gliding apparatus.

Reconstruct bat ancestry using fossil-calibrated mammal phylogenies and compare ancestral forelimb and membrane characters with extant and fossil gliders. Transitional gliding-adapted anatomy predating powered-flight characters supports the claim; evidence for a non-gliding ancestor or alternative functional sequence refutes it.

Place bats, colugos, and gliding rodents on a phylogeny and score the locomotor apparatus of the earliest fossil bats. Nesting of bats among gliding mammals, or early fossils built for gliding rather than flapping, would support derivation from a gliding apparatus; non-gliding nearest relatives plus early powered-flight fossils would refute descent from the living gliding groups. An extinct gliding stage with no fossil representative would remain untested.

obstacles: A fossil gap remains between non-volant insectivorous laurasiatherian ancestors and the earliest known Eocene bats (*Onychonycteris*), which already possessed powered flapping flight alongside primitive climbing/gliding limb proportions.
Soft-tissue wing membranes (patagia) are preserved only in exceptional Lagerstatten.
The earliest known bats were already capable of powered flight.
Soft flight membranes are rarely preserved and extant gliders are not necessarily ancestral analogues.
A gliding ancestor could be extinct and unsampled even if living gliders are not close relatives.
The membrane extending to the legs can be an adaptation for flight rather than a leftover of gliding.
Early bat fossils are few, so locomotor inferences rest on a small sample.

claims.label: Selecting one trait unconsciously modifies other correlated parts
claims.statement: Because of laws of correlation of growth, when man selects for and augments any peculiarity, he almost certainly also modifies other parts of the structure without intending to.

operationalizations.text: Estimate additive genetic covariance matrices (G-matrices) and correlated responses to directional artificial selection in domestic animal and plant breeding datasets; confirm if single-trait selection produces statistically significant changes in unselected traits predicted by genetic correlations.

Estimate genetic correlations and correlated responses between deliberately selected traits and unselected traits in breeding populations. Nonzero repeatable correlated responses support the claim; consistently independent traits would refute it.

Estimate genetic correlations, or correlated responses, between a selected target trait and traits that were not selection criteria, across breeding populations and crop evaluation trials. Widespread non-zero correlated change would support the expectation; a regular pattern of target traits changing alone would refute the 'almost certainly' clause.

obstacles: Hitchhiking of linked loci in small breeding populations can mimic developmental/pleiotropic correlation of growth.
Linkage can mimic pleiotropic correlation.
The phrase 'almost certainly' requires broad sampling.
Genetic-correlation matrices are published study by study rather than in one livestock-and-crop archive.
Mendelian pleiotropy over-represents genes of large effect relative to the slight variations Darwin emphasized.
Unintentional change can also come from drift and linkage, which mimic correlation of growth.
